regions.name: Mittelrhein
regions.summary: The Mittelrhein is the Rhine's gorge from Bingen north past Koblenz to the Siebengebirge near Bonn, one of the smallest of Germany's thirteen Anbaugebiete and Riesling country above all: about two thirds of its vines are Riesling, with Spätburgunder a distant second. The river has cut deep through the Rhenish Slate Mountains, so the vineyards cling to steep terraces of Devonian slate under castles, on the bends and in the side valleys that turn to the sun. The wines are taut, racy and stony, mostly dry or off dry, and keen enough in acidity to make good Sekt. Hold four facts: steep slopes on the Rhine, a continental climate, Riesling and slate.

terroir.climate: Cool continental, at about 50 degrees north, with cold winters and warm summers. The gorge is sheltered: the Hunsrück to the west and the Taunus to the east break the wind and keep off part of the rain, and below Koblenz the Eifel and the Westerwald do the same. Inside the gorge the river and the dark slate keep the steep, sun-facing walls warmer than the plateau above, so Riesling ripens slowly through a long autumn and keeps its acidity. Cold air drains off the steep slopes onto the river; a wet autumn and the rot it brings are the commoner hazard.
terroir.soils: Devonian slate, grey and blue, with greywacke and bands of quartzite: the rock of the Rhenish Slate Mountains. On the steep walls it weathers into thin, stony soil that drains at once and warms fast in the sun, and the vines root deep into the cracks of the rock. Loess and loam cover some of the gentler slopes and old river terraces, and at the northern end the Siebengebirge adds soils weathered from volcanic rock.
terroir.topography: For over 100 kilometres the Rhine runs north from Bingen to the edge of the Siebengebirge, cutting a narrow, winding gorge through the uplands with a castle on crag after crag. Vineyards sit on terraces held up by dry stone walls, on the outer side of the bends and at the mouths of side valleys, wherever a slope turns south, south-east or south-west; some pass 60 per cent. Below Koblenz the valley opens into the Neuwied basin before it narrows again on the way to the Siebengebirge.
terroir.water: The Rhine is the region's stove: a wide, deep river that stores warmth, throws reflected light up the slopes and softens the cold of the gorge, while its autumn mists keep the air moist. The Nahe joins it at Bingen, where the region begins, the Lahn at Lahnstein and the Mosel at Koblenz; further north the Ahr flows in from the west between Remagen and Sinzig.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: About two thirds of the vineyard: racy, light to medium bodied Riesling of green apple, citrus and a stony, slate edge, dry, feinherb or sweet, and a base for Sekt.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Labelled Spätburgunder and the second grape, about a tenth of the vines: light, fresh dry reds, and Blanc de Noir, Weissherbst and Sekt.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Also sold as Rivaner: soft, floral, early drinking white from the gentler sites.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.styles: A Trollinger and Riesling crossing that ripens more easily than Riesling, for fruity, off dry whites.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder: dry, creamy, apple and almond whites from a small share of the vineyard.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder: dry, round, pear and nut, a small share beside Riesling.

wines.note: Dry, light to medium bodied, with lime, green apple and a stony, smoky slate finish; serve it cold with river trout, smoked fish or asparagus.
Off dry, the sweetness balanced by the region's high acidity, with peach and citrus; a match for pork, ham or a gently spiced dish.
A dry Riesling from a VDP Grosse Lage such as Bacharach's Hahn: denser and firmer, built to age for a decade; open a young bottle early or decant it.
From late picked, sometimes botrytised grapes in good years: honey, apricot and lime held up by keen acidity; serve it with fruit tarts or blue cheese.
Crisp, citrus and apple, often made by the traditional method from the region's tart Riesling; an aperitif.
Light, dry Pinot Noir of red cherry and earth, served a little cool with duck, game birds or mushroom dishes.

made.viticulture: Almost everything is done by hand. The walls of the gorge are terraced and walled with dry stone, and on the steep walls the only help is often a winch or a small monorail track that carries tools and grapes. That labour, and the better living to be had in the towns and in tourism, emptied much of the old vineyard over the twentieth century: whole hillsides above the river have gone back to scrub and woodland, and the region keeps shrinking while the wine from what survives keeps improving. What remains is mostly Riesling on the slopes that face the sun, trained on single stakes on the steep terraces or on wires where the slope allows. Riesling ripens late here, picked through October and into November, which gives a long hang time, high acidity and moderate sugar. In warm years noble rot brings Auslese and, rarely, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese. Storms wash the thin slate soil off the terraces, and the walls need constant repair.
made.winemaking: Riesling is fermented cool in stainless steel or in old oak casks, the Fuder and the Stück of the Rhine and the Mosel, often slowly and with the cellar's own yeasts. Most wine is made trocken or feinherb, with Kabinett and Spätlese often left with some sweetness to balance the acidity, and alcohol stays moderate. Qualitätswein may be chaptalised when the grapes fall short; Prädikatswein never. The keen acidity has long made Mittelrhein Riesling a base for Sekt, and many estates bottle a Riesling Sekt by the traditional method. Spätburgunder is fermented on its skins and aged in barrel for dry reds, or pressed at once for a white Blanc de Noir or briefly macerated for a Weissherbst rosé. Grosses Gewächs Riesling is dry, from hand picked grapes, and released no earlier than the year after the harvest.

law.classification: The Mittelrhein is one of Germany's thirteen Anbaugebiete under the wine law of 1971, the protected designation of origin on a Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein label. It spans two federal states: almost all of it lies in Rhineland-Palatinate, and its small northern tip in the Siebengebirge in North Rhine-Westphalia. It holds two Bereiche, Loreley and Siebengebirge. Grosslagen gather its villages, and every true vineyard is an Einzellage, named after its village with an -er ending: Bacharacher Hahn. The Prädikat ladder applies as everywhere, by must weight at picking, and trocken, halbtrocken and feinherb say how dry the wine is. The VDP's members classify their own leading sites: Bacharach's Hahn and Wolfshöhle are VDP Grosse Lagen, whose dry Riesling is the Grosses Gewächs. The federal amendment of January 2021 makes Grosses Gewächs and Erstes Gewächs legal terms and makes a Grosslage carry the word Region, binding in full from the 2026 vintage.
tiers: Quality wine from the region; may be chaptalised; passes the official tasting and carries an AP number.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight at picking, never chaptalised; Kabinett and Spätlese are the common rungs here.
The larger of the two Bereiche: the gorge from the Bingen end down past Koblenz, in Rhineland-Palatinate.
The northern tip around Königswinter, opposite Bonn, in North Rhine-Westphalia.
The growers' top classified sites, among them Bacharach's Hahn and Wolfshöhle; the dry Riesling from one is the GG.
labels: An old Rhenish word for slate or a rock face, found in site names such as Feuerlay.
A castle; Schloss is a castle or palace, used on a label as château is in France.
Off dry in the grower's own words, with no legal sugar limit; common on Mittelrhein Riesling.
Village with -er, then the vineyard: the Hahn at Bacharach; every Einzellage is named this way.
Quality sparkling wine from one named region, such as a Mittelrhein Riesling Sekt.
Estate bottled, from the estate's own vines and cellar.

places.name: Bereich Loreley
places.note: The larger of the two Bereiche, named for the rock at St. Goarshausen: every vineyard in Rhineland-Palatinate, from the gorge at the Bingen end down past Koblenz to the villages below the Neuwied basin.

places.name: Bacharach
places.note: A walled medieval town on the left bank under Stahleck castle, the leading wine town of the southern gorge, with steep slate vineyards on the Rhine and behind the town.

places.name: Hahn
places.note: A steep slate slope on the Rhine just north of the town, inclined at up to about 70 per cent: a VDP Grosse Lage known for firm, long lived Riesling.

places.name: Wolfshöhle
places.note: A steep slate site above the town beside the Posten, below Stahleck castle, and a VDP Grosse Lage.

places.name: Heylesen Werth
places.note: An island in the Rhine at Bacharach planted with vines, registered as a single vineyard of its own: a rare river island site.

places.name: Steeg
places.note: A village in a side valley running west from Bacharach, known for the St. Jost, a steep slate site sheltered from the river's winds.

places.name: Oberwesel
places.note: A walled town of towers on the left bank, upstream of the Lorelei: the Oelsberg above the Rhine, and the Engehöll, a side valley of slate.

places.name: Kaub
places.note: A right-bank village facing the toll castle of Pfalzgrafenstein, which stands on its island in the river; steep slate slopes face the Rhine.

places.name: Loreley
places.note: The slate cliff on the right bank at St. Goarshausen, some 130 metres above the river where the Rhine narrows and bends hard; the heart of the gorge and of its Romantic legend, with vineyards at St. Goar and St. Goarshausen.

places.name: Boppard
places.note: A Roman town on the left bank where the Rhine swings round a great loop; the steep slate wall on its outer side, the Bopparder Hamm, is a long run of vineyard turned to the sun.

places.name: Bopparder Hamm
places.note: The slate amphitheatre of the loop, divided into named sites, Feuerlay, Mandelstein and Ohlenberg among them, giving riper, fuller Riesling than the narrow reaches upstream.

places.name: Leutesdorf and Hammerstein
places.note: Right-bank villages below Koblenz and the Neuwied basin, where the valley narrows again; slate and greywacke slopes face south-west over the river.

places.name: Bereich Siebengebirge
places.note: The northern tip of the region around Königswinter, across the Rhine from Bonn and in North Rhine-Westphalia: a few slopes on the weathered volcanic rock of the Seven Mountains, under the Grosslage name Petersberg.

places.name: Drachenfels
places.note: The castle-crowned volcanic hill above Königswinter, with Riesling and Spätburgunder on its lower slopes at about 50.7 degrees north.

producers.name: Ratzenberger
producers.why: A Steeg estate known for Riesling from the St. Jost and the Wolfshöhle and for traditional method Riesling Sekt.

producers.name: Lanius-Knab
producers.why: An Oberwesel estate whose dry and off dry Rieslings come from the Engehöll and the Oelsberg.

producers.name: Weingart
producers.why: A Spay estate making precise, mostly dry Riesling from the Bopparder Hamm, the Feuerlay among its sites.

exam: Place the Mittelrhein: the Rhine gorge from Bingen, opposite the Rheingau's Rüdesheim, north past Koblenz to the Siebengebirge near Bonn.
Hold the four facts the Court gives: steep slopes along the Rhine, a continental climate, Riesling as the main grape, slate soil.
Know Riesling as about two thirds of the vineyard and Spätburgunder as the second grape.
Explain why Riesling ripens this far north: steep, sun-facing slate walls, the river's reflected light and stored warmth, the shelter of the uplands.
Find on a map Bacharach, the Lorelei at St. Goarshausen, Boppard and Koblenz, where the Mosel joins the Rhine.
Apply the national ladder to a Mittelrhein label: Qualitätswein, the Prädikate by must weight, trocken and feinherb, the VDP's Grosses Gewächs.
Asked from Premier Cru: the two Bereiche, Loreley and Siebengebirge; Bacharach's Hahn and Wolfshöhle as Grosse Lagen; the Bopparder Hamm and its sites; Lorch, in the gorge but legally Rheingau.
Asked from Grand Cru: the island vineyard Heylesen Werth and the volcanic Drachenfels at the northern tip.
traps: Lorch, on the right bank inside the gorge, is legally Rheingau; Bingen at the gorge's mouth is Rheinhessen.
The Mittelrhein is not the Mittelmosel: the Middle Mosel is a stretch of the Mosel region.
Koblenz is where the Mosel meets the Rhine, but the Mosel region's vineyards lie upstream along the Mosel, not in the Mittelrhein.
The Ahr, whose valley joins the Rhine from the west near Remagen, is a separate region and grows mostly red; the Mittelrhein is Riesling country.
Loreley is a rock and a Bereich; the siren who sings on it belongs to Romantic poetry, not history.
A Grosslage name reads like a vineyard but covers several villages; from the 2026 vintage it must carry the word Region.
Feinherb is not a legal term: it says off dry without a number.

cards.b: The Rhine gorge from Bingen to the Siebengebirge near Bonn: steep slopes of slate, a continental climate, and Riesling as the main grape.
From Bingen, where the Nahe joins and the Rheingau's Rüdesheim faces it, north past Koblenz to the Siebengebirge across from Bonn.
Riesling, about two thirds; Spätburgunder, about a tenth; then Müller-Thurgau, Kerner and the white Pinots.
Devonian slate with greywacke and quartzite on the steep walls; loess and loam on gentler slopes; volcanic soils in the Siebengebirge.

cards.f: Why Riesling ripens in the gorge
cards.b: Steep, sun-facing slate walls; the Rhine's stored warmth and reflected light; shelter from the Hunsrück and Taunus. Ripening is slow and late, so acidity stays high.

cards.f: The Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site
cards.b: Inscribed by UNESCO in 2002: about 65 kilometres of the gorge from Bingen and Rüdesheim to Koblenz, castles, towns and terraced vineyards together.
Loreley, the gorge and the villages below Koblenz in Rhineland-Palatinate; Siebengebirge, the northern tip around Königswinter in North Rhine-Westphalia.
The Hahn, a steep slate slope on the Rhine north of the town, and the Wolfshöhle, above the town below Stahleck castle.
The steep slate wall on the outer side of the Rhine's great loop at Boppard, split into named sites such as Feuerlay, Mandelstein and Ohlenberg.
Trocken: cold, with trout, smoked fish or asparagus. Kabinett or Spätlese feinherb: with ham, pork or gentle spice. Auslese: with fruit tarts or blue cheese.

questions.q: Which rock underlies most of the Mittelrhein's vineyards?
questions.exp: Devonian slate, with greywacke and quartzite, forms the Rhenish Slate Mountains through which the Rhine cuts its gorge. Limestone and chalk belong to other regions, and granite only to patches elsewhere in Germany.

questions.q: Which grape covers about two thirds of the Mittelrhein's vineyard?
questions.exp: Riesling fills about two thirds of the region, with Spätburgunder a distant second; Müller-Thurgau and Kerner are small shares, and Silvaner belongs to Franken and Rheinhessen.

questions.q: Which climate category does the Court give the Mittelrhein?
questions.exp: The Mittelrhein is cool continental, with cold winters and warm summers, softened by the Rhine and the shelter of the gorge.

questions.q: Which river joins the Rhine at Koblenz, inside the Mittelrhein?
questions.exp: The Mosel meets the Rhine at Koblenz. The Lahn joins at Lahnstein, just upstream, the Nahe at Bingen where the region begins, and the Neckar far to the south at Mannheim.

questions.q: Which volcanic hill range marks the northern end of the Mittelrhein, across the river from Bonn?
questions.exp: The Siebengebirge, the Seven Mountains, around Königswinter is the region's northern tip and its own Bereich, in North Rhine-Westphalia.

questions.q: How many Bereiche does the Mittelrhein hold?
questions.exp: Two: Loreley, which covers the gorge and the villages below Koblenz, and Siebengebirge, the northern tip in North Rhine-Westphalia.

questions.q: In which Mittelrhein town does the VDP Grosse Lage Hahn lie?
questions.exp: The Hahn is a steep slate slope on the Rhine just north of Bacharach. Boppard has the Bopparder Hamm, Oberwesel the Oelsberg, and St. Goarshausen sits under the Lorelei.

questions.q: To which wine region does Lorch belong, though it lies on the right bank inside the Mittelrhein's gorge?
questions.exp: Lorch lies beyond the Rhine's bend at Assmannshausen, in the gorge, but it is legally part of the Rheingau, with steep slate and lean Riesling.
